rule.description: Agentic workflows should not be vulnerable to path injection attacks
rule.name: jssecurity:S8707
rule.full_description: Agentic workflows should not be vulnerable to path injection attacks
rule.help:
Why is this an issue?

Large Language Models (LLMs) attempt to get out of their diverse sandboxes to get their tasks done, sometimes in ways which could break unexpected systems. In addition to that, malicious users can apply direct or indirect prompt injection techniques, prompting it to use special characters.

In agentic workflows, these LLMs orchestrate tasks by invoking external tools, including CLI programs. For this reason, providing unchecked ability to an LLM to access the file system straight from the CLI may turn out to be dangerous.

What is the potential impact?

A web application is vulnerable to path injection and an attacker is able to exploit it.

The files that can be affected are limited by the permission of the process that runs the application. Worst case scenario: the process runs with root privileges on Linux, and therefore any file can be affected.

Below are some real-world scenarios that illustrate some impacts of an attacker exploiting the vulnerability.

Override or delete arbitrary files

The injected path component tampers with the location of a file the application is supposed to delete or write into. The vulnerability is exploited to remove or corrupt files that are critical for the application or for the system to work properly.

It could result in data being lost or the application being unavailable.

Read arbitrary files

The injected path component tampers with the location of a file the application is supposed to read and output. The vulnerability is exploited to leak the content of arbitrary files from the file system, including sensitive files like SSH private keys.

How to fix it in Node.js

Code examples

The following code is vulnerable to path injection because the CLI tool constructs a file path from its input arguments without proper validation.
When this tool is invoked by an AI agent, an attacker who manipulates the agent can read or overwrite arbitrary files on the system.

Noncompliant code example

const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

const filePath = process.argv[2];

const data = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8'); // Noncompliant

Compliant solution

The standard mitigation against path traversal is to canonicalize and validate untrusted data with business-specific directories, such as /data/uploads/.

In the context of a CLI application loosely coupled to its environment, prevent LLMs from escaping the directory from which it was invoked:

const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

function safePath(filePath) {
  const resolved = fs.realpathSync(filePath);
  const baseDir = fs.realpathSync(process.cwd());
  if (resolved !== baseDir && !resolved.startsWith(baseDir + path.sep)) {
    throw new Error(`path '${filePath}' is outside the allowed directory`);
  }
  return resolved;
}

const filename = process.argv[2];

const data = fs.readFileSync(safePath(filename), 'utf8');

How does this work?

Canonical path validation

If it is impossible to use secure-by-design APIs that do this automatically, the universal way to prevent path injection is to validate paths constructed from untrusted data:

  1. Ensure the target directory path ends with a forward slash to prevent partial path traversal, for example, /base/dirmalicious starts with /base/dir but does not start with /base/dir/.
  2. Resolve the canonical path of the file by using methods like `fs.realpathSync`. This will resolve relative path or path components like ../ and removes any ambiguity regarding the file’s location.
  3. Check that the canonical path is within the directory where the file should be located.

Important Note: The order of this process pattern is important. The code must follow this order exactly to be secure by design:

  1. data = transform(user_input);
  2. data = normalize(data);
  3. data = sanitize(data);
  4. use(data);

As pointed out in this SonarSource talk, failure to follow this exact order leads to security vulnerabilities.

In the example compliant code, the canonical path of the target file is resolved using fs.realpathSync, which resolves any ../ path components. The resulting absolute path is then checked to ensure it starts with the expected base directory, preventing access to files outside of it.

Pitfalls

Partial Path Traversal

When validating untrusted paths by checking if they start with a trusted folder name, ensure the validation string contains a path separator as the last character.
A partial path traversal vulnerability can be unintentionally introduced into the application without a path separator as the last character of the validation strings.

For example, the following code is vulnerable to partial path injection because the string baseDir does not end with a path separator:

const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');

const baseDir = '/data/resources';
const filename = process.argv[2];
const filePath = path.join(baseDir, filename);
const canonicalPath = fs.realpathSync(filePath);

if (!canonicalPath.startsWith(baseDir)) {
  console.error('Access denied');
  process.exit(1);
}

const data = fs.readFileSync(canonicalPath, 'utf8');

This check can be bypassed because "/data/resources-secret".startsWith("/data/resources") returns true. Thus, for validation, "/data/resources" should actually be "/data/resources/".

Do not use path.resolve as a validator

The official documentation states that if any argument other than the first is an absolute path, any previous argument is discarded.

This means that including untrusted data in any of the parameters and using the resulting string for file operations may lead to a path traversal vulnerability.

Resources

Documentation

  • OWASP - Input Validation Cheat Sheet
  • GTFOBins - list of Unix binaries that can be used to bypass local security restrictions
  • LOLBAS - list of Windows binaries that can be used to bypass local security restrictions

rule.description: Confidential data should not be logged
rule.name: jssecurity:S8689
rule.full_description: Confidential data should not be logged
rule.help:
Why is this an issue?

Application logs are rarely treated with the same security discipline as databases or configuration files. They are typically stored in plain text, forwarded to centralized log aggregation platforms (Splunk, Datadog, ELK), retained for months or years, and accessible to a wide range of infrastructure engineers, operations staff, and automated systems.

Confidential data entails:

  • Credentials, API keys, tokens
  • Personally identifiable information
  • Business Sensitive information
  • And so on.

Inadvertently logging any of this kind of data within application logs or observability metrics exposes them to lower-trust environments and increases the risk of compromise. Any system or person with read access to those logs gains access to the secret, often without the application developer being aware.

What is the potential impact?

Credential harvesting

An attacker who gains read access to log files through another attack vector such as breach of logging infrastructure or stolen DevOps credential can extract every secret that was ever logged. A single leaked API key or password may grant access to databases, cloud accounts, or third-party services with permissions far beyond what the attacker originally obtained.

PII exposure and regulatory liability

Personally identifiable information logged even briefly may constitute a violation of GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, or other regulations. Log retention policies often mean PII persists far longer than the business need that caused it to be logged. Regulatory fines and mandatory breach notification obligations follow.

Audit trail poisoning

Log files are also the primary source of evidence during incident response. Credentials appearing in logs make it impossible to determine whether a later access was legitimate or the result of the leaked secret being reused. Non repudiation is lost, and incident response teams may be chasing false leads or missing the real attack vector entirely.

How to fix it in Express.js

Code examples

The following Express.js login handler logs the user’s password on every authentication attempt. The password is permanently recorded in the application’s log output.

Noncompliant code example

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/login', (req, res) => {
  const { username, password } = req.body;
  console.log(`Login attempt: user=${username} password=${password}`); // Noncompliant
});

Compliant solution

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/login', (req, res) => {
  const { username, password } = req.body;
  console.log(`Login attempt: user=${username}`);
  // ... authentication logic
});

How does this work?

Log what happened, not what the data was

A log entry should record that an authentication attempt occurred, not the credential used. Design log statements to capture outcomes and identifiers (username, request ID, timestamp, status code) rather than the values of sensitive inputs.

Use structured redaction

When using a structured logging library, configure it to redact sensitive fields automatically rather than relying on developers to omit them manually. Most production logging libraries support this:

// pino — built-in redaction
const logger = pino({ redact: ['password', 'token', 'authorization'] });
logger.info({ username, password }, 'Login attempt'); // password is redacted

// winston — custom formatter
const { createLogger, format, transports } = require('winston');
const redactSecrets = format((info) => {
  const sensitiveKeys = /password|secret|token|key|auth|credential/i;
  for (const key of Object.keys(info)) {
    if (sensitiveKeys.test(key)) info[key] = '[REDACTED]';
  }
  return info;
});
const logger = createLogger({
  format: format.combine(redactSecrets(), format.json()),
  transports: [new transports.Console()]
});
logger.info({ username, password }, 'Login attempt'); // password is redacted

Replace values with hashes or prefixes for traceability

When you need to correlate log entries with a specific credential (e.g., to trace which API key made a request), log a truncated prefix or a one-way hash rather than the full value.

Resources

Documentation

  • OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Logging Cheat Sheet
  • AWS Documentation - AWS Secrets Manager best practices

Standards

  • CWE - CWE-532 - Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
  • CWE - CWE-200 - Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
  • CWE - CWE-359 - Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

rule.description: Prefer COPY over ADD for copying local resources
rule.name: docker:S7029
rule.full_description: Prefer COPY over ADD for copying local resources
rule.help:
In Dockerfiles, it is recommended to use the COPY instruction over the ADD instruction for copying local resources. The COPY instruction is more straightforward and less prone to errors, making it a better choice for copying local files and directories into a Docker image.

Why is this an issue?

Using the ADD instruction instead of COPY for local resources in Dockerfiles can lead to several issues, including unexpected behavior, increased complexity, and security risks. The ADD instruction has additional features that can introduce unintended side effects, such as automatically extracting compressed files and fetching remote resources. This can make the behavior of the instruction less predictable and harder to understand or even lead to security issues, if, for example, due to a typo in the source path, the ADD instruction could fetch a remote resource instead of copying a local file.

If you only need to copy local files or directories into your Docker image, it is recommended to use the COPY instruction instead. Only use the ADD instruction when you need its additional features, such as fetching remote resources or extracting compressed files. See also the rule {rule:docker:S7026} for more information on using the ADD instruction to fetch remote resources.

How to fix it

Code examples

Noncompliant code example

FROM ubuntu:20.04
ADD ./app /app

Compliant solution

FROM ubuntu:20.04
COPY ./app /app

Resources

Documentation

  • {rule:docker:S7026} - Use ADD instruction to retrieve remote resources
  • Docker Docs - Building best practices

message.text:
Replace this ADD instruction with a COPY instruction.

See more on SonarQube Cloud

This can make the behavior of the instruction less predictable and harder to understand or even lead to security issues, if, for example, due to a typo in the source path, the ADD instruction could fetch a remote resource instead of copying a local file.

If you only need to copy local files or directories into your Docker image, it is recommended to use the COPY instruction instead. Only use the ADD instruction when you need its additional features, such as fetching remote resources or extracting compressed files. See also the rule {rule:docker:S7026} for more information on using the ADD instruction to fetch remote resources.

How to fix it

Code examples

FROM ubuntu:20.04
ADD ./app /app

Compliant solution

FROM ubuntu:20.04
COPY ./app /app
